new_entities.name: Daycare attendance during the first year of life

edges.effect_quant: Across birth cohorts, daycare attendance in the first year reliably shifts respiratory infections earlier and makes them more frequent during infancy. The best long prospective data show clear short-term excesses in upper respiratory infections, otitis, and other infectious morbidity among children who enter group care early.
edges.population: infants attending group daycare during the first 12 months of life compared with home-cared infants
edges.mechanism: Group childcare increases contact density with other children during a period of immunologic immaturity, which raises exposure to respiratory viruses and bacterial otopathogens. The tradeoff is not subtle: early clustering of infections is exactly what daycare changes most consistently in infancy.
edges.summary: Daycare attendance during the first year of life increases respiratory infectious burden in infancy. The signal is strongest for upper-respiratory and ear infections, but broader birth-cohort work also shows more general infectious morbidity around the period of early daycare entry.
edges.caveats: This edge is about infections during infancy, not whether early daycare is good or bad overall for development. Later childhood may show some catch-down in infection frequency, but that does not erase the higher burden in the first year of life.

evidence.citation: OliveiraPD et al 2019 J Pediatr (Rio J)
